notes.title: Electric current
points: Current is the flow that carries charge from one point to another per unit time.
By convention, current is taken to flow from the positive (+) terminal to the negative (‑) terminal.
The unit of current is the ampere (A); 1 A = 1 C/s (coulomb per second).

notes.title: Potential difference (Voltage)
points: Voltage is the work done in moving a unit charge from one point to another.
It is measured in volts (V); 1 V = 1 J/C (joule per coulomb).
A voltage source (such as a battery) drives the flow of current.

notes.title: Ohm's law
points: At a constant temperature, current (I), voltage (V) and resistance (R) are directly proportional: V = I × R.
If R remains constant, the I‑V graph is a straight line.
Ohm's law applies only to materials whose resistance does not change with temperature (ohmic materials).

notes.title: Resistance and resistivity
points: Resistance (R) measures how much a material opposes the flow of current; its unit is the ohm (Ω).
Resistivity (ρ) is an intrinsic property of the material; its unit is Ω·m.
R = ρ × L / A, where L = length (m) and A = cross‑sectional area (m²).

notes.title: Factors affecting resistance
points: Material: different substances have different ρ values (e.g., copper < iron).
Length (L): resistance increases directly with length.
Area (A): resistance decreases inversely with cross‑sectional area.
Temperature (T): for most metals, ρ increases with temperature, so R also increases.

notes.title: Series combination of resistors
points: In a series connection, all resistors are linked end‑to‑end.
The same current flows through each resistor: I_series = I_total.
Voltage across each resistor follows V = I × R and is divided among them.
Equivalent resistance: R_eq = Σ R_i.

notes.title: Parallel combination of resistors
points: In a parallel connection, the two ends of each resistor are joined to the same two points.
Voltage across each resistor is the same: V_parallel = V_total.
Current divides among the branches; total current is Σ I_i.
Equivalent resistance: 1/R_eq = Σ (1/R_i).

notes.title: Heating effect of current and Electric power
points: Heat produced by the flow of current is called Joule heating; its magnitude is P = I² × R (watts).
Everyday devices such as electric heaters, toasters, bulbs and electric kettles operate on this principle.
Electric power P = V × I, and can also be written as P = I²R or P = V²/R.
The unit of energy is the joule (J); the practical unit for electrical energy is the kilowatt‑hour (kWh), where 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

teach.heading: Fundamental understanding of current and voltage
teach.explain: Current is the flow that transports charge, while voltage is the driving force that makes the charge move. They are measured separately: current in amperes and voltage in volts.
teach.example: For example, connect a 12 V battery across a 2 Ω resistor; the current will be I = V/R = 12/2 = 6 A.

teach.heading: Ohm's law and its application
teach.explain: At a constant temperature, V, I and R are directly proportional. This relationship can be verified in the laboratory by building a simple circuit.
teach.example: For instance, a 9 V battery connected to a 3 Ω resistor gives I = 9/3 = 3 A, and the voltage across the resistor V = I × R = 3 × 3 = 9 V, matching the source voltage.

teach.heading: Causes of resistance and calculation
teach.explain: Resistance depends on the material, length, cross‑sectional area and temperature. Using the formula R = ρL/A, the resistance of any uniform wire can be calculated.
teach.example: For example, a copper wire 1 m long with a cross‑section of 1 mm² has ρ = 1.68×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, so R = (1.68×10⁻⁸ × 1) / (1×10⁻⁶) = 0.0168 Ω.

teach.heading: Rules for series and parallel combinations
teach.explain: In series, the current is the same through all resistors and the voltage is divided; in parallel, the voltage is the same across each resistor and the current is divided. These rules help simplify complex circuits.
teach.example: For example, connect 2 Ω and 6 Ω in series, then place this series combination in parallel with a 3 Ω resistor. The series resistance is 8 Ω; then 1/R_eq = 1/8 + 1/3, giving R_eq ≈ 2.18 Ω.

teach.heading: Heating effect and electric power
teach.explain: Heat generated by current flow is given by P = I²R. Power can also be expressed as P = V×I. This principle is used in heating appliances.
teach.example: For example, a 1500 W heater operates on 230 V. The current is I = P/V = 1500/230 ≈ 6.52 A, and the resistance is R = V/I ≈ 35.3 Ω.

steps: Series resistance R_series = 2 Ω + 6 Ω = 8 Ω

practice.q: If a current of 3 A flows through a 10 Ω resistor, what is the voltage?
practice.explanation:
V = I × R
V = 3 A × 10 Ω
V = 30 V

practice.q: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in series. What is the equivalent resistance?
If the above two resistors are connected in parallel, what is the equivalent resistance?
Given ρ = 5×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, L = 1 m, A = 2 mm², find the resistance.
A 60 W bulb is connected to 120 V. What is the current through it?
In a series circuit the total current is 2 A and the total resistance is 15 Ω. What is the total voltage?
practice.explanation:
V = I × R
V = 2 A × 15 Ω
V = 30 V

practice.q: Which statement about parallel combination is correct?
options: Voltage across each resistor is different
Equivalent resistance is greater than each individual resistance
Current through each resistor is the same
Equivalent resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance
practice.explanation: In parallel, 1/R_eq = Σ(1/R_i), so R_eq is always less than the smallest R_i.

practice.q: A 2 kW heater operates on 220 V. Find its resistance.
A 100 W bulb runs for 5 hours. How much energy does it consume?
practice.explanation: Energy = P × t = 100 W × 5 h = 500 Wh = 0.5 kWh

practice.q: When the temperature of a metal wire increases, what generally happens to its resistance?
practice.explanation: For metals, resistivity ρ typically rises with temperature, so R also increases.

mistakes: Current does not 'end' in a series circuit; it remains the same throughout the entire circuit.
Resistance does not depend only on current; it depends on length, area, material and temperature.
In a parallel circuit, the equivalent resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance, not greater.
revision: Ohm's law: V = I × R, valid only at constant temperature.
R = ρL/A; ρ is an intrinsic property of the material.
In series, R_eq = ΣR, current is the same, voltage divides.
In parallel, 1/R_eq = Σ(1/R), voltage is the same, current divides.
Heating effect: P = I²R; everyday devices such as heaters and bulbs use this.
Electric power: P = V I = I²R = V²/R, unit W.
When temperature rises, the resistance of a metal increases; for insulators it may decrease.
